> Full public documentation for Solana Developer Platform — all page content for AI and agent ingestion.

## Docs

### What is SDP?
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/introduction

> One API in front of interchangeable providers for building on Solana.

SDP puts each of its modules behind one stable API in front of interchangeable providers. Operations use project-scoped authentication.

| Module | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Issuance** | Deploy, mint, burn, freeze, pause, and seize tokens built on Token-2022 |
| **Custody** | Provision and operate Solana wallets through interchangeable custody providers |
| **Payments** | Move funds onchain — transfers, batches, recurring payments, and payment requests |
| **Ramps** | Move between fiat and onchain funds through interchangeable ramp providers |
| **Compliance** | Screen wallets and transactions against your regulatory program |
| **Asset profiles** | Issued-asset identity and metadata, and the public token metadata URI |

## Background

Institutional capital is moving onchain: [$35 billion in tokenized real-world assets](https://app.rwa.xyz/) across public blockchains, [$3.2 billion of it on Solana](https://app.rwa.xyz/networks/solana), and [tokenized stocks](https://app.rwa.xyz/stocks) — where Solana settles most trading volume — as the fastest-growing slice.

Assets at this scale need regulated custody, enforceable compliance, and auditable controls. SDP provides them as one API, so bringing an asset onchain does not require a team of Solana developers.

## Core Features

<Steps>
<Step>
### Unified Programming Interface

SDP puts one stable API in front of the Solana ecosystem's providers, so you integrate once and swap or add providers without changing your code. The same call works for every custody provider. The `provider` field is the only thing that changes.

<Tabs items={["JavaScript", "Python", "curl"]}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```javascript title="create-wallet.js"
const response = await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: "Bearer sf_...",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    provider: "privy",
    label: "Treasury wallet",
  }),
});
const wallet = await response.json();
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Python">
```python title="create_wallet.py"
import requests

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets",
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer sf_..."},
    json={"provider": "privy", "label": "Treasury wallet"},
)
wallet = response.json()
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "provider": "privy", "label": "Treasury wallet" }'
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>
</Step>
<Step>
### Wallet Custody

Provision signing wallets through integrated custody providers, so your team never handles private keys. Hosted keys never leave the provider's MPC or TEE infrastructure and SDP only handles the signed transaction. Local development keys are encrypted at rest with `AES-256-GCM` using per-organization derived keys, and every signing request passes authentication, permission and allowed-operation checks before it executes.

- **Built on `@solana/keychain`**

   The unified Solana signing interface. Every custody backend is a keychain adapter behind the same signing API, which is what makes providers interchangeable.

- **[Grants by module](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#grants-by-module)**

   Limit what an API key may do. A key holds an explicit list of actions, such as reading one module or executing in another, and every other route is refused before it runs.

- **Scoped custody configuration**

   Custody settings resolve per project, then organization, then environment, so different teams can run different providers side by side.
</Step>
<Step>
### Onchain Transfers

SDP exposes unified endpoints for onchain transfers, built on official Solana program implementations like [Subscriptions](https://github.com/solana-program/subscriptions) and [Solana Pay](https://github.com/solana-foundation/pay). These power Recurring Payments, Payment Requests, and Batch Transfers within SDP.

<Tabs items={["Recurring Payments", "Payment Requests", "Batch Transfers"]}>
<Tab value="Recurring Payments">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/recurring-payments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..." \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: recurring-subscriber-42" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "sourceCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
    "counterpartyId": "cp_...",
    "counterpartyAccountId": "cpa_...",
    "token": "USDC",
    "amount": "25.00",
    "periodHours": 720
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Payment Requests">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/requests \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "walletId": "privy_wallet_123",
    "token": "USDC",
    "amount": "25.00",
    "expiresAt": "2026-08-31T00:00:00.000Z"
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Batch Transfers">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfer-batches \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..." \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: payroll-2026-06-30" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "externalId": "payroll_2026_06_30",
    "sourceCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_example",
    "token": "USDC",
    "recipients": [
      {
        "externalId": "payroll_row_001",
        "counterpartyId": "cp_...",
        "counterpartyAccountId": "cpa_...",
        "amount": "25.00"
      }
    ]
  }'
```

See [Payments](/docs/payments) for transfers, batches, and payment requests.

<Step>
### Audit Trails

Every sensitive operation is recorded automatically. Each entry captures the acting user or API key, the resource touched, success or failure, client IP, user agent, request id, and secret-redacted metadata, and is queryable per organization.

| Area                    | Recorded events                                                                    |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| API keys                | Create, revoke, and rotate, for both organization and project-scoped keys          |
| Custody                 | Provider configuration, wallet provisioning, and credential lifecycle changes      |
| Transactions & signing  | Signing requests, submissions, and failed submissions                              |
| Organization & access   | Members, invitations, projects, and project membership             |
| Counterparties          | Counterparty and Counterparty Account changes                                      |
</Step>
</Steps>

## Developing with SDP

### Overview
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/developing-with-sdp

> The interfaces, environments, and conventions you build against.

SDP exposes two interfaces that operate over the same backend and enforce the same grants, wallet scopes, and audit trails:

- **Dashboard** — browser-based UI for setup, token management, and compliance operations. Sign in with email, Google, or GitHub.
- **REST API:** programmatic access for backend integrations. Routes authenticate with an API key in the `Authorization` header.

Everything the dashboard does is available through the API. Build against the API for automation and integrations; use the dashboard to set up your organization, inspect state, and perform one-off operations.

## Environments

Authenticated environments are a property of the **project**, not of individual requests. Every tenant resource and API key belongs to a project and inherits that project's environment.

| Environment  | Network      |
| ------------ | ------------ |
| `sandbox`    | devnet       |
| `production` | mainnet-beta |

A key's format does not name its environment: the project it belongs to does.

Both environments expose the same route shapes. Develop and test authenticated integrations against a sandbox project, then switch to production by swapping your API key.

## Response conventions

Every successful response wraps its payload in a `data` envelope with request metadata:

```json
{
  "data": { ... },
  "meta": { "requestId": "req_...", "timestamp": "2026-07-31T12:00:00.000Z" }
}
```

Errors return a machine-readable `code` alongside a human-readable `message`:

```json
{
  "error": { "code": "INVALID_API_KEY", "message": "Invalid API key" }
}
```

Include the `requestId` when reporting an issue — it links your request to our internal traces and audit records.

## Execution model

SDP executes custody operations by building, signing, and submitting with the configured custody wallet.

---

### Idempotency
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/developing-with-sdp/idempotency

> Retry mutations safely with the Idempotency-Key header. Required on the routes that move money, and accepted on the mutations listed below.

Clients time out, connections drop and workers die mid-run. Send an `Idempotency-Key` header so a retry returns the first attempt's answer instead of doing the work twice.

```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..." \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: 0192f8a4-6c1e-7d4b-8f3a-b7e52c8d9f0a" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ ... }'
```

## Where keys apply

**Required.** These routes move money. A request without a key returns `400 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED`, and nothing runs.

- `POST /v1/payments/transfers`
- `POST /v1/payments/transfer-batches`
- `POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments`
- `PATCH /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}` (an edit to an active schedule signs and broadcasts a replacement subscription)
- `POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}/activate`
- `POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}/cancel`
- `POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}/collect`
- `POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}/resume`

**Accepted.** The key is optional, and honored when sent.

- Wallets: `POST /v1/wallets`, `POST /v1/wallets/initialize`, `POST /v1/wallets/signer-check`, `PATCH /v1/wallets/{walletId}`, `DELETE /v1/wallets`
- Subscription plans and subscriptions: `POST /v1/payments/subscription-plans`, `PATCH /v1/payments/subscription-plans/{planId}`, `POST /v1/payments/subscriptions`
- Counterparties: `POST`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` on `/v1/counterparties` and on counterparty accounts
- Compliance: `POST /v1/compliance/address-screenings`

**Not used.** `POST /v1/payments/transfer-batches/estimate` moves and stores nothing. The subscription `prepare-*` routes and subscription-plan `prepare-create` return an unsigned transaction bound to a fresh blockhash, which a stored replay would hand back after it expired. Neither reads the key.

Modules with their own key handling say so on their pages.

## Choosing a key

- A key is 1–255 printable ASCII characters. Anything else returns `400`.
- Generate one key per logical operation (a UUIDv4 or UUIDv7 works well), store it with the operation before you send it, and send the same key on every retry of that operation.
- A new operation needs a new key, even when its request is identical to an earlier one.
- Keys are scoped to your organization, project, HTTP method and route, and bound to the credential that sent them. The same key value on two different routes is two separate keys.

A money request, saved with its key before the first send and retried under that key:

```typescript title="send-transfer.ts"
// Save the key with the operation first, so a restarted worker retries under it.
const payout = await db.payouts.create({ ...input, idempotencyKey: crypto.randomUUID() });

async function sendTransfer(payout: Payout): Promise<Response> {
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= 8; attempt++) {
    let response: Response;
    try {
      response = await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          Authorization: "Bearer sf_...",
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
          "Idempotency-Key": payout.idempotencyKey,
        },
        body: JSON.stringify(payout.request),
      });
    } catch {
      // The connection dropped: the transfer may have run, so retry under the same key.
      await backoff(attempt);
      continue;
    }
    if (!(await isRetryable(response))) return response;
    await backoff(attempt, response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
  }
  throw new Error(`Transfer ${payout.id} is still unanswered: retry later with the same key`);
}

async function isRetryable(response: Response): Promise<boolean> {
  // A money route answers a same-key retry after a 5xx from the record the first attempt wrote.
  if (response.status >= 500 || response.status === 429) return true;
  if (response.status !== 409) return false;
  const { error } = await response.clone().json();
  return error?.code === "IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_FLIGHT";
}

function backoff(attempt: number, retryAfter?: string | null): Promise<void> {
  const ms = Math.max(Number(retryAfter ?? 0) * 1000, 250 * 2 ** attempt);
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
}
```

Every retry above sends the same body and the same key. Don't change the request to "fix" a retry: a different request under the key is `422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`.

## What a retry returns

Access is checked before the key on every request, so a retry passes exactly the checks a new request passes, and a request refused for access never claims the key.

| Situation | Response |
| --- | --- |
| Same key, same request, original finished | The original status and body, with the response header `Idempotent-Replayed: true`. |
| Same key, original still running | `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_FLIGHT` with `Retry-After`. Wait, then retry with the same key. |
| Same key, original never recorded its outcome (it crashed) | Until 15 minutes plus the route's lease have passed since the original was sent (about 16 minutes, or about 20 for transfer batches), `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_FLIGHT` with `Retry-After`, as if it were still running. After that, transfers, transfer batches, recurring payments and `POST /v1/wallets` take over and answer from the record the original wrote. A batch whose original stopped before sending some recipients answers with those recipients `failed`: they were never sent, so send them again in a new batch with a new key. Every other route returns `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN` with no `Retry-After`, to this and every later retry with the key: read the resource with `GET` to see whether it ran, then send again with a new key. |
| Same key, different request or different credential | `422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`. Nothing runs. |
| Same key, but the credential has since lost access to the wallet or resource | `403`. The stored response is not returned. |
| Original was refused with `400`, `401`, `403`, `409` or `429` before it wrote anything | Nothing was stored. Fix the cause and retry with the same key; the request runs again. |
| A transfer or transfer batch failed after writing its record (for example `400 TRANSACTION_FAILED`, or `409` for a signer mismatch) | Stored: the same error, with `Idempotent-Replayed: true`. After 24 hours the record answers with the same status and code. The key is spent: send the request again with a new key to try again. |
| A recurring-payment action failed | An action refused before it sent anything leaves the schedule as it was. If a cancel or resume sent its transaction and confirming it then failed, SDP keeps the attempt and the schedule stays `canceling` or `resuming` until the attempt is recovered; poll `GET /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}`. A `400`, `401`, `403`, `409` or `429` (such as `TRANSACTION_FAILED`) is not stored, and a `5xx` is not replayed, so a same-key retry runs the action again. Any other `4xx`, such as `422 SIGNING_REJECTED` or `404`, is stored and replayed with `Idempotent-Replayed: true` for 24 hours; send a new key to try again sooner. |
| A recurring-payment action meets another key's unfinished attempt on the schedule | Cancel, resume and collect return `409` (already processing), not stored; read the schedule with `GET`. An interrupted collect finishes on its own from the transaction SDP saved before sending it. An interrupted activate, cancel or resume is resumed in the background from the last step SDP recorded; SDP first reads each step it may already have sent from the chain, and a step is not sent again when the chain shows it landed. An interrupted `PATCH` resumes only when that `PATCH` is retried with its key (see below). A `PATCH` may finish that attempt and then applies its own change. |
| A keyed recurring-payment cancel, resume or `PATCH` changes nothing (such as canceling a canceled schedule) | It still records its attempt, so a same-key retry, even after 24 hours, is answered from it and never runs over a later change. |
| Original returned a `5xx` | Stored and replayed: use a new key to try again. The routes that move money are the exception: a same-key retry runs again and answers from the record the first attempt wrote, so it never sends twice. That answer also carries `Idempotent-Replayed: true`. |

"Same request" means the same path, query parameters, body and credential. Recipient order in a transfer batch, and `"1.0"` versus `"1"` for an amount, do not change the request.

Keys are scoped to the credential that sent them. A rotated API key is a new credential: for 24 hours after the original request, a retry under the new API key with the old `Idempotency-Key` gets `422`; after that, the old key's record is gone and the same retry runs as a new request and can move money again, as can any retry under a new `Idempotency-Key`. So after any API key rotation, read the resource with `GET` (for example `GET /v1/payments/transfers` or `GET /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}`) to learn whether the original request ran, and never resend a money request under the new credential without checking first.

An organization that has been deleted or has lost production access is refused before the key is read: `401` or `403`, even for a retry of a request that completed.

## Replays are snapshots

A replay returns the response as it was first sent: a transfer stored as `processing` replays as `processing`. To see current state, read the resource with `GET`. Never re-send a request to learn its outcome.

When the answer comes from the original record instead (a same-key retry after a `5xx`, or after the 24-hour window), it reflects that record as it stands now. A recurring-payment lifecycle action answered this way returns the schedule as it is, which may still be mid-transition; poll `GET /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}` until it settles. An update left `updating` is not finished in the background: retry the `PATCH` with the same key. Until the interrupted attempt is 15 minutes old, that retry gets `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_FLIGHT` with `Retry-After`; after that, it resumes from the last step SDP recorded, and a step is not sent again when the chain shows it landed.

## Retention

Keys are kept for 24 hours after the original request. After that, a same-key retry on most accepted routes starts a new request. On the routes that move money, the record the first attempt wrote still holds its key, so a late retry is answered from that record, or refused if the request differs; a failed transfer answers with the status and code it failed with.

## Creating wallets

With a key, SDP never records a second wallet for one `POST /v1/wallets` key: a retry returns the wallet an earlier attempt recorded, within 24 hours or after, and the same key on a different request returns `422`. Privy and Coinbase CDP also receive a request id derived from the key, so they dedupe the request at the provider. A provider failure is stored as a `503` for 24 hours, and a new key is a new provider request. A `503` can mean the provider created the wallet before the error. Only Privy and Coinbase CDP dedupe on the request id, so with any other provider, an ambiguous failure that left no SDP wallet row makes even the same `Idempotency-Key` a new provider request once its 24-hour record has expired. Before any retry after an ambiguous failure, whatever key you use, check `GET /v1/wallets` and, if the wallet is not there, the provider account itself. The provider request id and the lookup of the recorded wallet both include the credential, so after an API key rotation, once the key's 24-hour record has expired, the same `Idempotency-Key` under the new API key no longer finds the earlier attempt: it is a new provider request and can create a second wallet. After rotating the API key, list wallets with `GET /v1/wallets` and check the provider account before retrying a create.

## The dashboard and the Postman collection

The dashboard sends a key on every request to the routes that require one, and keeps it until it gets a definitive answer, so a retried click never moves money twice.

The [Postman collection](/docs/reference/postman-collection) saves one key per operation for the required routes (the `idempotencyKey.<operationId>` collection variable) and follows the dashboard's rule for money routes. It mints the key only when the variable is unset and clears it only on a `2xx` that shows the payment final, a replayed refusal, or a `422` other than `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`. A `2xx` that shows the transfer, batch or schedule still `pending` or `processing` keeps the key: poll it with `GET` instead of sending a new one, and clear the variable once it is final. Every other answer keeps it too, so resending reuses the key: a timeout, a `5xx`, a `409` (in flight or outcome unknown), a `429`, and a `400`, `401` or `403` refusal, after which the original may still have run. A `422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED` means only that the request differed from the key's original: restore the original request to retry it. Clear the variable yourself to start a new operation, after checking with `GET` that the original settled.

## Recommendations

- Send a key on every mutation that accepts one, not only where it is required.
- Retry timeouts, connection errors and `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_FLIGHT` with backoff, reusing the key.
- Treat `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN` as final for that key: check with `GET`, then use a new key.
- After a `5xx`, retry with the same key on the routes that move money; elsewhere, use a new key.
- Outside a key rotation, treat `422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED` as a bug in your client: the key was attached to two different operations.
- Persist the returned resource ID before moving to the next operation, so a restarted worker can resume without guessing.

### Authentication
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/developing-with-sdp/authentication

> Authenticate API requests with project-scoped API keys, layered with grants, wallet bindings, and network controls.

SDP layers independent controls onto a single API key — grants, wallet bindings, and IP allowlist — so a key grants exactly the access its integration needs, and no more.

Authenticated API requests carry an API key in the `Authorization` header:

```bash title="Terminal"
curl https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..."
```

The `Bearer` prefix is optional — a raw key in the `Authorization` header is also accepted.

## Key scope

Keys are issued per **project** and inherit that project's environment: a key from a sandbox project reaches devnet, one from a production project mainnet-beta. The key itself does not name its environment; the dashboard shows it next to each key. A key can only reach the wallets, tokens, and payments of the project it was issued for; there is no cross-project or organization-wide key.

## Authorization layers

A request must clear every layer that is configured on its key:

| Layer | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| **Grants** | The actions (`module.verb`) the key may perform. Each route needs exactly one; see [Grants by module](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#grants-by-module) |
| **Wallet bindings** | Restrict which custody wallets the key can operate, each binding with its own permission list |
| **IP allowlist** | Optional IPv4/IPv6/CIDR ranges the key may be used from, set on the key; an organization-wide list under **Settings** applies to every key on top. Neither restricts signed-in dashboard members |

## Errors

Authentication and authorization failures are always machine-distinguishable: the code says what kind of refusal it is, and a 403 names what it is missing in `error.details`.

| Condition | Status | Code | `error.details` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No API key on a keyed-only request | 401 | `UNAUTHORIZED` | |
| Malformed or unknown key | 401 | `INVALID_API_KEY` | |
| Key has been revoked, its organization was deleted or suspended, or its project was archived | 401 | `REVOKED_API_KEY` | |
| Key past its expiry or rotation deadline | 401 | `EXPIRED_API_KEY` | |
| Request origin not in the key's or the organization's IP allowlist | 403 | `FORBIDDEN` | `reason: "ip_not_allowed"` |
| Route only a signed-in dashboard member may use, such as managing keys, members or the organization | 403 | `FORBIDDEN` | `reason: "human_session_required"` |
| Key lacks the route's action, or the action a signature it asks for needs | 403 | `INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS` | `action` names the missing action |
| SDP refused to sign for the request (see below) | 403 | `FORBIDDEN` | `reason` names why |
| Per-key rate limit exceeded | 429 | `RATE_LIMITED` | |

### Signing refusals

SDP decides again each time it signs on a key's behalf, so a change to the key or the organization applies to the next signature, including one later in the same request. Nothing is signed or sent on refusal. `error.details.reason` is one of:

| `reason` | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `wallet_out_of_scope` | The custody wallet is outside the key's wallet scope |
| `wallet_purpose` | The custody wallet's purpose may not send payments: only a `transfer` wallet can be the source of a transfer, batch, recurring payment or offramp |
| `principal_not_live` | The key was revoked, expired, or passed its rotation deadline during the request |
| `organization_inactive` | The organization is suspended or deleted |
| `production_not_enabled` | The project is a production project and the organization does not have production access |
| `project_not_found` | The project no longer exists |
| `principal_missing` | No credential is attached to the movement |

A key without the action a signature needs is refused with `INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS` and `error.details.action`, exactly as at the route.

Requests are rate limited per key; the standard tier allows 100 requests per minute.

See [Manage API Keys](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys) for creating, rotating, and revoking keys.

---

### Manage API Keys
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys

> Create, rotate, and revoke API keys with explicit grants by module, a signing wallet scope, and zero-downtime rotation.

Create, rotate, and revoke the API keys that authenticate SDP API requests. Each key belongs to a project, inherits its environment, and holds an explicit list of grants plus optional controls — see [Authentication](/docs/developing-with-sdp/authentication) for how those layers are enforced.

Keys are credentials, not administrators: they are created, changed, rotated, and revoked only by a signed-in member of your organization in the dashboard. An API key cannot manage keys, the organization, its members, or project members, whatever it is granted; it is refused with `403 FORBIDDEN` and `error.details.reason` set to `human_session_required`.

The full secret is returned exactly once — at creation and at rotation. SDP stores only a keyed hash of the secret and the key ID; a lost key cannot be recovered, only rotated or replaced. Every key tracks `lastUsedAt` so you can identify stale credentials before revoking them.

## Key format

Keys use the shared Solana Foundation format, `sf_<key id>_<secret><checksum>`:

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `<key id>` | 16 hex characters. Not secret: safe to log, and shown in the dashboard to tell keys apart |
| `<secret>` | 43 base62 characters (256 random bits) |
| `<checksum>` | 6 base62 characters, so a mistyped key is refused at once and secret scanners can match a leaked one |

The format does not name an environment: a key reaches the network of the project it was created in (sandbox: devnet, production: mainnet-beta). Keys created before this format, prefixed `sk_test_` or `sk_live_`, keep working until they are revoked.

## Grants by module

Every API route performs exactly one **action**, named `module.verb`, and a key may call a route only when it holds that action. A key holds an explicit list of grants: there is no role and no wildcard.

| Verb | What it allows |
| --- | --- |
| `read` | View the module's records |
| `manage` | Create and edit records reversibly: drafts, pausing, cancelling |
| `execute` | Anything irreversible or that leaves SDP: on-chain transactions, provider calls, moving money, and changing where money goes, such as a payout destination or a recurring amount |
| `enforce` | Token enforcement: freeze, pause, seize, force-burn, allowlist |
| `authority` | Transferring or revoking a token's authorities |

`manage` and `execute` each include the same module's `read`. Nothing else implies another action: `execute` does not include `manage`, and a grant on one module gives nothing on another. These are the actions a key can be granted on this deployment:

| Module | Actions | Covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `transfers` | `transfers.read`, `transfers.execute` | Single transfers from a custody wallet |
| `transfer_batches` | `transfer_batches.read`, `transfer_batches.execute` | Batches of transfers, and their estimates |
| `payment_requests` | `payment_requests.read`, `payment_requests.manage` | Payment requests and their payment links |
| `counterparties` | `counterparties.read`, `counterparties.manage`, `counterparties.execute` | Counterparties, their accounts, and provider requirements |
| `transactions` | `transactions.read` | The unified transaction list; each row also needs the read of its own module |
| `recurring` | `recurring.read`, `recurring.manage`, `recurring.execute` | Recurring payments, subscription plans and subscriptions |
| `wallets` | `wallets.read`, `wallets.manage`, `wallets.execute` | Custody wallets and their balances |
| `compliance` | `compliance.execute` | Address screening |
| `projects` | `projects.read` | Projects and provider availability |
| `onramp` | `onramp.read`, `onramp.execute` | On-ramp currencies, estimates and quotes |
| `offramp` | `offramp.read`, `offramp.execute` | Off-ramp currencies, estimates and quotes |
| `ramp_transfers` | `ramp_transfers.manage` | Ramp transfer cancellation and sandbox simulation |
| `issuance` | `issuance.read`, `issuance.manage`, `issuance.execute`, `issuance.enforce`, `issuance.authority` | Tokens, templates, asset profiles, and their on-chain actions |
| `dvp` | `dvp.read`, `dvp.manage`, `dvp.execute` | Delivery-versus-payment trades |
| `private_channels` | `private_channels.read`, `private_channels.manage`, `private_channels.execute` | Private channel instances, channels and movements |
| `helius_rings` | `helius_rings.read`, `helius_rings.manage`, `helius_rings.execute` | Helius Rings wallets, rings and operations |

Some actions are never granted to a key, because keys are credentials, not administrators: key, member, organization and project administration, and every provider, credential or connection setup (`configure`). A create or update naming one is refused with `400`. So is a grant on a module this deployment does not run; a key that already holds one keeps it when an update sends it back.

A request without the route's action is refused with `403 INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS`, and `error.details.action` names the missing action. Nothing runs or is recorded on refusal. Grants are read on every request, so a change applies to the key's next request.

When you create a key you can grant only actions you hold yourself. **Everything** in the dashboard writes out every action available when the key is created; an action added to SDP later is not granted to existing keys.

## Wallet access

A key's wallet scope decides which custody wallets SDP may sign with on its behalf:

| `walletScope` | Signs with |
| --- | --- |
| `all` | Every custody wallet in the key's project |
| `selected` | Only the wallets listed in `walletIds`. With none listed, the key signs with no custody wallet; SDP's fee sponsor is outside wallet scope |

`walletIds` are custody wallet ids, the `id` (`cwlt_…`) that `GET /v1/wallets` returns, not a provider's wallet id. A key keeps the exact wallets you listed: a wallet created later, even one reusing a provider id, is never added.

SDP checks the scope each time it signs, together with the key's grants and whether it is still active, so a narrowed scope or a revoked key stops the next signature, including one later in the same request. A signature outside the scope is refused with `403 FORBIDDEN` and `error.details.reason` set to `wallet_out_of_scope`; nothing is signed or sent.

The scope narrows what a key may sign with, not what it may read. A `selected` key's wallet list (`GET /v1/wallets`) and wallet detail reads show only its wallets; every other read, such as transfers, batches and recurring payments, covers the whole project. Give a separate project to an integration that must not see another's records.

For recurring payments the scope also bounds writes that sign nothing. A `selected` key may create, change, cancel, activate, collect or resume only a recurring payment whose source wallet it lists, and may move one only to another listed wallet, because whoever activates a pending payment signs the terms it was last given. Anything else is refused with `wallet_out_of_scope` before it is recorded. Reading and listing recurring payments still cover the whole project.

The dashboard starts a key that holds any `execute` action on **Selected wallets**, so it can sign with nothing you did not give it; choose **All wallets** to widen it.

## Recurring payments outlive the key

A recurring payment is collected on schedule as its own mandate, not as the key or member that activated it. SDP still checks that the payment is active, that it pays from its own source wallet, and that the organization may move money. Revoking or narrowing the key that activated it does not stop it, so rotating a key never interrupts a customer's schedule.

## Create a key

1. Navigate to **API keys** in the sidebar. You start with an empty list.

   ![API keys page with no keys yet](/images/getting-started/api-keys-empty.png)

2. Click **New API key** in the top right, then fill in the key details:
   - **Name** — a descriptive label (e.g., "CI deploy key")
   - **Permissions** — a checkbox per verb for each module (Read, Manage, Execute); ticking Manage or Execute includes Read. **Everything** ticks every offered action
   - **Wallet access** — All wallets or Selected wallets
   - **Expiration (optional)** — date/time picker
   - **Allowed IP addresses (optional)** — one IPv4 or IPv6 address or CIDR range per line; empty allows any address. Edit the key to change or clear it

   ![Create API key modal](/images/getting-started/api-key-create.png)

3. Click **Continue**, review the summary, and click **Create key**.

   ![Review API key modal](/images/getting-started/api-key-review.png)

4. Click **Copy** on the **API key generated** modal and save the key — it will not be shown again.

   ![API key generated modal, full key redacted](/images/getting-started/api-key-generated.png)

5. Dismiss the modal. The key now appears in the table with its prefix, grants, environment, and status.

   ![API keys list with one active key](/images/getting-started/api-keys-list.png)

The key belongs to the project you create it in and inherits that project's environment.

## Rotate a key

Rotation replaces the secret without an availability gap: the new key is a fresh record that clones the old key's grants, IP allowlist, and wallet scope, while the old key keeps working until its grace deadline. During the grace period both keys are valid; after it, the old key fails with `EXPIRED_API_KEY`.

1. In the API keys table, open the **Actions** dropdown next to the key and click **Rotate key (24h grace)**.

   ![Actions dropdown showing Rotate key and Delete key options](/images/getting-started/api-key-rotate.png)

2. Copy the new key value from the generated key modal — it is shown once.

## Revoke a key

Open the **Actions** dropdown next to the key and click **Delete key**. The key stops working on its next request and cannot be restored. Deleting a rotated key during its grace period ends the overlap early: the replacement keeps working.

If the key may be compromised, also cancel the recurring payments it activated: send `"cancelRecurringPayments": true` with the revocation. A recurring payment answers to the key that activated or last resumed it, or that last changed its source wallet, recipient, token, amount or period: that change re-authorizes where its money goes. Changing only its metadata or next collection date does not. The response lists the recurring payments it canceled and any it could not, which you can cancel one by one.

### Set Up Your Organization & Projects
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/guides/setup-organization

> Set up your SDP organization and see how projects scope work within it.

Every SDP user works through an **organization** — a team workspace containing one or more **projects**, each a provisioned environment with its own API keys, wallets, and members. This guide creates your organization and covers how projects scope your resources.

### 1. Sign up

Go to [platform.solana.com](https://platform.solana.com) and click **Dashboard**. On the sign-in screen, click **Sign up** to create a new account.

![SDP sign-in screen with Sign up link](/images/getting-started/sign-in.png)

Enter your email address and a password to create your account.

![Create your account screen](/images/getting-started/create-account.png)

After signing in you'll be prompted to set up your organization. Upload a logo and enter your organization name, then click **Continue**.

![Setup your organization screen](/images/getting-started/setup-organization.png)

If you already have an organization, the **Organization Switcher** in the top-left of the sidebar lets you switch between them or create a new one.

<img src="/docs/images/getting-started/org-switcher.png" alt="Organization Switcher dropdown" width="436" style={{ display: "block", maxWidth: "100%" }} />

### 3. Organize with projects

A **project** is a provisioned environment within your organization — sandbox or production-style — with its own API keys, wallets, tokens, and members, so teams don't share the same wallet and token surface. See the [Projects API reference](/docs/reference/api/projects) for managing them programmatically.

### 4. Next steps

### Set Up Wallets
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/guides/setup-wallets

> Initialize a custody provider and create wallets for signing transactions.

A **custody wallet** is a Solana keypair whose key is held and signed for by a custody provider — SDP routes signing requests to whichever provider holds the wallet's key. Initialize a provider, then create wallets for transfers and other onchain operations.

## Supported providers

| Provider | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **Privy** | Embedded wallet infrastructure platform |
| **Fireblocks** | Digital asset infrastructure company |
| **Coinbase CDP** | Embedded wallets for developers |
| **Para** | Wallet and authentication suite |
| **Turnkey** | Non-custodial wallet infrastructure platform |
| **DFNS** | Digital asset wallet infrastructure |
| **Anchorage** | Regulated institutional crypto custody |

<Tabs items={["Dashboard", "API"]}>
<Tab value="Dashboard">

### 1. Navigate to Wallets

Open the sidebar and click **Wallets**. If you haven't linked your organization yet, complete the [organization setup](/docs/guides/setup-organization) first.

### 2. Choose a custody provider

The Wallets page shows all supported providers, each with a **New wallet** button. Pick the provider that fits your setup.

![Wallets page showing custody provider cards](/images/getting-started/wallet-providers.png)

### 3. Create the wallet

Click **New wallet** on your chosen provider. In the modal, enter a label for the wallet and click **Create wallet**.

If you have connected your own account with that provider, choose the account the wallet is created in: the provider's Managed account (when the project has one) or one of your active connections. The choice appears as soon as one active connection exists, and nothing is preselected: SDP has no default custody, so every wallet names where it lives.

<img src="/docs/images/getting-started/wallet-create-modal.png" alt="New wallet modal" width="696" style={{ display: "block", maxWidth: "100%" }} />

### 4. View your wallet

After provisioning, the wallet card appears on the Wallets page with its address, wallet ID, and balance.

![Wallets page after wallet creation](/images/getting-started/wallet-created.png)

To create additional wallets, click **Create Wallet** in the top right and repeat the process.

### 5. Provider capabilities

Each provider supports a different set of operations shown as capability chips:

- **Transfers** — can sign payment transactions
- **Compliance** — can sign freeze/unfreeze instructions

</Tab>
<Tab value="API">

#### 1. Initialize the provider from the dashboard

Initializing a custody provider is provider setup (`wallets.configure`), and no API key can hold a `configure` action. An organization admin initializes it once per project, signed in to the dashboard (see the **Dashboard** tab); the dashboard calls `POST /v1/wallets/initialize` with that session. The same call made with an API key returns `403` with `details.action` set to `wallets.configure`.

Production projects use BYOK only. `POST /v1/wallets/initialize` sets up Managed custody, so in a Production project it returns `403` with `details.reason` set to `custody_mode_not_allowed`. Connect your own provider account to the project from the dashboard instead, then create wallets in that connection with `connectionId` using an API key that holds `wallets.manage`:

```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "connectionId": "cconn_123",
    "label": "Treasury wallet"
  }'
```

#### 2. Create additional wallets

Every wallet names the provider account it lives under: `provider` for the provider's Managed account, or `connectionId` for a connection your project added. Send exactly one of them. There is no default account to fall back to.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "provider": "privy",
    "label": "Treasury wallet",
    "purpose": "transfer"
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="create-wallet.ts"
const response = await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Authorization": "Bearer sf_...",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    provider: "privy",
    label: "Treasury wallet",
    purpose: "transfer",
  }),
});
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="CreateWallet.java"

    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sf_...")

        {
          "provider": "privy",

          "purpose": "transfer"
        }"""))
    .build();
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

The `purpose` field is optional metadata in the API. The current dashboard create-wallet flow does not expose wallet-purpose selection.

</Tab>

</Tab>

Every operation that signs names its wallet; there is no default wallet. Transfers take the wallet's `id` (`cwlt_…`) as `sourceCustodyWalletId`. Other modules name it the same way (their pages say which field). An API key limited to selected wallets lists the same `id` in `walletIds`.

```typescript title="transfer-request.ts"
const body = {
  sourceCustodyWalletId: "cwlt_123", // `id` from GET /v1/wallets
  destination: "7xKXz...9fGh",
  token: "9aBCd...4eEf",
  amount: "100.00",
};
```

## Tokens

### Tokenize an Asset
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/tokens/tokenize-an-asset

> Map a real-world asset to the right SDP token model, authorities, and implementation flow.

Use this page when you want to issue a stablecoin, tokenized security, loyalty token, or any other asset through Solana Developer Platform. It walks you from business decision to the first API call.

## Choose a token model

Pick the **Tokenization Template** that matches your asset's compliance and operational requirements:

| Asset model | Template | Typical controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fiat-backed stablecoin | `stablecoin` | Mint authority, freeze authority, pausable, permanent delegate |
| Tokenized security or RWA | `tokenized-security` | Allowlist required, freeze authority, pausable, permanent delegate |
| Loyalty, rewards, or utility token | `custom` | Manually selected extensions |
| Non-standard asset | `custom` | Manually selected extensions |

**Custody wallets** hold your token's authorities by default, so SDP can execute deploy, mint, and compliance actions without external signing.

## Compliance enforced onchain

Create tokens from pre-built templates (stablecoin, tokenized security) or configure your own using Token-2022 extensions. Deploy, mint, burn, and manage supply through the dashboard or API.

Those same extensions are what make compliance enforceable onchain. Freeze individual accounts, pause token activity, seize tokens, and manage each token's **Token Access Control** list for regulated issuance flows. Selected compliance actions accept reason or memo fields for audit trails. Every enforcement action is one POST on the same token surface.

<Tabs items={["JavaScript", "Python", "curl"]}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```javascript title="compliance-action.js" rotate-token-ops
const response = await fetch(
  "https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_abc123/freeze",
  {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: "Bearer sf_...",
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(operationParams),
  },
);
const result = await response.json();
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Python">
```python title="compliance_action.py" rotate-token-ops
import requests

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_abc123/freeze",
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer sf_..."},
    json=operation_params,
)
result = response.json()
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal" rotate-token-ops
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_abc123/freeze \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "$OPERATION_PARAMS"
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Audit trail

Issuance and compliance actions are recorded in the organization's audit log alongside every other sensitive operation (see [What is SDP?](/docs/introduction)):

| Area                    | Recorded events                                                                    |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Token issuance          | Deploy, mint, burn, force-burn, supply changes, and authority updates              |
| Compliance actions      | Freeze, unfreeze, pause, unpause, seize, and Token Access Control changes          |
| Asset profiles          | Asset profile changes                                                              |

## Idempotency

Execute-mode issuance operations consume the `Idempotency-Key` header ([Idempotency](/docs/developing-with-sdp/idempotency)) in a namespace of their own:

| Domain | Operations | Key namespace |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Issuance | Execute-mode deploy, mint, burn, force-burn, freeze, thaw, pause, unpause, seize, and authority transfer | Per organization, shared across **all** issuance operations and tokens |

The issuance namespace is organization-wide: reusing a key for a different issuance operation, even on a different token, returns 409.

Each step links to its own guide with UI and API instructions:

## Core API endpoints

| Method | Endpoint | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/v1/issuance/templates` | List available token templates |
| `POST` | `/v1/issuance/tokens` | Create a token definition |
| `POST` | `/v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/deploy` | Deploy to Solana |
| `POST` | `/v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/mint` | Mint new supply |
| `POST` | `/v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/burn` | Reduce supply |
| `POST` | `/v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/allowlist` | Add a Token Access Control entry |
| `POST` | `/v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/freeze` | Freeze an account |
| `POST` | `/v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/pause` | Pause all transfers |
| `POST` | `/v1/payments/transfers` | Transfer tokens |

See the full schema in the [Issuance API reference](/docs/reference/api/issuance) and [Payments API reference](/docs/reference/api/payments).

## Operational constraints

- A token must be **created** before deployment, and **deployed** before minting or transfer.
- If the token is paused, minting and transfer operations are unavailable until it is unpaused.
- Freeze and unfreeze flows accept a holder wallet address; SDP derives the associated token account automatically.
- SDP operations require the relevant authority on a custody wallet. If an authority has been rotated outside SDP, rotate it back to a controlled wallet before deploying, minting, or running compliance actions.

### Create a Token
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/tokens/create-a-token

> Define a new token using a template or custom configuration.

Token creation defines your token's metadata, extensions, and operational rules. The token is saved in SDP but **not yet deployed** onchain — see [Deploy a Token](/docs/tokens/deploy-a-token) for the next step.

![Empty Issuance page with a create card](/images/tokens/token-list-empty.png)

## Templates

| Template | Decimals | Key extensions | Use case |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `stablecoin` | 6 | Permanent delegate, pausable | USD-backed tokens |
| `tokenized-security` | 8 | Permanent delegate, pausable, scaled UI amount, allowlist required | Regulated assets |
| `custom` | 9 | None — you choose | Full control |

```typescript title="create-token.ts"
  body: JSON.stringify({
    name: "Acme Dollar",
    symbol: "ACME",
    decimals: 6,
    description: "USD-backed stablecoin",
    template: "stablecoin",
    signingCustodyWalletId: "cwlt_abc123",
    requiresAllowlist: false,
    isMintable: true,
    isFreezable: true,
  }),
});
```

For a custom token, omit `template` or set it to `"custom"` and pass `overrides.extensions`:

```typescript title="create-custom-token.ts"
body: JSON.stringify({
  name: "Game Coin",
  symbol: "GAME",
  decimals: 0,
  template: "custom",
  signingCustodyWalletId: "cwlt_abc123",
  overrides: {
    extensions: {
      pausable: {},
      transferFee: { basisPoints: 50, maxFee: "1000" },
    },
  },
  isMintable: true,
  isFreezable: false,
}),
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>
</StepPanel>

</Step>

<Step number={4} title="Confirm creation">

The token is saved in SDP with status `pending`. Nothing has been written to Solana yet.

<StepPanel>
<Tabs items={["UI", "API"]} groupId="how-it-works">
<Tab value="UI">

A success toast confirms creation. The token appears in the **Issuance** list with a `Draft` badge.

![Issuance list showing the newly created token with a Draft badge](/images/tokens/token-list-draft.png)

Open the token to see its detail page. The status shows **Not deployed** and a **Deploy** button is available to move to the next step.

![Token detail page showing Not deployed status and Deploy button](/images/tokens/token-detail-pending.png)

</Tab>
<Tab value="API">

A successful response returns the new token object:

```typescript title="create-token.ts"
const { data } = await res.json();
// data.token.id     — save this; used in all subsequent calls
// data.token.status — "pending"
// data.token.signingCustodyWalletId — exact wallet selected for deployment
```

The token is not yet onchain. Pass `data.token.id` to [Deploy a Token](/docs/tokens/deploy-a-token).

</Tab>
</Tabs>
</StepPanel>

</Step>

</HowItWorks>

---

### Deploy a Token
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/tokens/deploy-a-token

> Deploy a created token to the Solana blockchain.

After [creating a token](/docs/tokens/create-a-token), deploy it onchain. Deployment creates the mint account on Solana and signs the deployment with the exact SDP Wallet selected for execution.

## Prerequisites

- A token in `pending` status
- The exact SDP Wallet `id` returned by `GET /v1/wallets` (for example, `cwlt_*`)

## How it works

<HowItWorks>

<Step number={1} title="Open the deploy action">

Locate the token you want to deploy. Deployment is irreversible — the mint account and its configured authorities are created onchain.

<StepPanel>
<Tabs items={["UI", "API"]} groupId="how-it-works">
<Tab value="UI">

In the **Issuance** list, click the token with a `Pending` badge to open its detail page.

The **Deploy** button appears in the token header and in the fund management panel.

![Token detail page showing Not deployed status and Deploy button](/images/tokens/token-detail-pending.png)

</Tab>
<Tab value="API">

You need the `tokenId` returned when you created the token. If you don't have it, list your tokens:

```bash title="Terminal"
curl https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..."
```

Note the token `id` (e.g., `tok_abc123`) — required for all deploy and post-deploy calls. Also list your wallets and use the wallet record's `id`, not its provider-specific `walletId` or public key:

```bash title="Terminal"
curl https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..."
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>
</StepPanel>

</Step>

<Step number={2} title="Deploy the token">

SDP signs and submits the deploy transaction using `signingCustodyWalletId`. If you supply it here, it overrides the pending draft's execution wallet; if you omit it, SDP uses the value stored on the draft. One of those values is required. An override changes the deployment signer and historical attribution, but it does not rewrite immutable authority values already captured in the token's configuration.

<StepPanel>
<Tabs items={["UI", "API"]} groupId="how-it-works">
<Tab value="UI">

Click **Deploy**. A modal shows the signer wallet that will authorize the transaction. Review the wallet ID and public key, then click **Deploy now**.

![Deploy token modal showing the signer wallet details](/images/tokens/token-deploy-modal.png)

A confirmation prompt asks you to confirm the on-chain submission. Click **Deploy now** to proceed.

![Deploy token confirmation dialog](/images/tokens/token-deploy-confirm.png)

SDP submits the transaction to Solana and polls for confirmation. The page updates automatically when deployment completes.

</Tab>
<Tab value="API">

```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_abc123/deploy \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: deploy-acme-001" \
  -d '{"signingCustodyWalletId":"cwlt_abc123"}'
```

```typescript title="deploy-token.ts"
const res = await fetch(
  "https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_abc123/deploy",
  {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: "Bearer sf_...",
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Idempotency-Key": "deploy-acme-001",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({ signingCustodyWalletId: "cwlt_abc123" }),
  }
);
const { data } = await res.json();
// data.token.mintAddress — the onchain mint address
```

Always pass an `Idempotency-Key` — retrying with the same key after a network error prevents double-deployment.

</Tab>
</Tabs>
</StepPanel>

</Step>

<Step number={3} title="Confirm deployment">

Once the transaction is confirmed, the token is active and ready for minting and transfers.

<StepPanel>
<Tabs items={["UI", "API"]} groupId="how-it-works">
<Tab value="UI">

The token status badge changes from `Not deployed` to the onchain mint address. The detail page shows Mint and Burn actions in the Operations tab, and a confirmed deploy transaction in the Transactions table.

![Deployed token detail page with mint address, Operations tab, and confirmed deploy transaction](/images/tokens/token-deployed.png)

</Tab>
<Tab value="API">

The deploy response includes the confirmed state:

```typescript title="deploy-token.ts"
// data.token.status      — "active"
// data.token.mintAddress — e.g., "AcMeXYZ..."
// data.token.signingCustodyWalletId — exact wallet used for deployment
```

After deployment, `signingCustodyWalletId` is historical deployment attribution. Mint and admin actions resolve their current on-chain authority, while a standard burn uses its exact source wallet; none use the deployment wallet as a fallback.

Fetch the token at any time to verify:

```bash title="Terminal"
curl https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_abc123 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..."
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>
</StepPanel>

</Step>

</HowItWorks>

---

### Mint and Burn
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/tokens/mint-and-burn

> Increase or decrease token supply by minting to an address or burning from an account you control.

After [deploying a token](/docs/tokens/deploy-a-token), you can mint new tokens to any address and burn tokens from accounts you control. Force-burn lets admins burn from any account without the holder's signature.

## Prerequisites

- A deployed token with status `active`
- The `issuance.execute` grant — or `issuance.enforce` for force-burn
- For standard burn, the exact SDP Wallet `id` returned by `GET /v1/wallets` (for example, `cwlt_*`)

## How it works

<HowItWorks>

<Step number={1} title="Select the token and action">

Open the token you want to manage. Mint and burn are both available from the token detail page.

<StepPanel>
<Tabs items={["UI", "API"]} groupId="how-it-works">
<Tab value="UI">

In the **Issuance** list, click an active token to open its detail page.

The **Fund management** panel shows the current supply with two primary actions: **Mint** and **Burn**.

![Token Operations tab showing Mint and Burn actions](/images/tokens/token-deployed.png)

</Tab>
<Tab value="API">

All supply operations share this URL pattern:

```text title="Endpoints"
POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/mint
POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/burn
POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/force-burn
```

The `amount` field is a decimal string in **UI units** (human-readable token amounts). `"1"` means one token; `"1.5"` means one and a half. SDP converts to on-chain base units using the token's `decimals`.

`signingCustodyWalletId` always means the exact SDP Wallet `id`, not a provider-specific `walletId` or public key. It is required for a standard burn because that wallet owns and signs for the source. For mint and force-burn it is optional, but when supplied it must control the current mint or permanent-delegate authority. When omitted, SDP requires exactly one accessible wallet to match that live authority. Later actions never fall back to the token's deployment wallet.

</Tab>
</Tabs>
</StepPanel>

</Step>

<Step number={2} title="Mint tokens">

Issue new tokens to a destination address. SDP derives the associated token account automatically.

<StepPanel>
<Tabs items={["UI", "API"]} groupId="how-it-works">
<Tab value="UI">

In the **Mint** form:

- **Destination** — wallet address to receive the new tokens
- **Amount** — in human-readable units (e.g., `1.0`)
- **Memo** — optional, recorded onchain

Click **Mint**. A modal shows the signer wallet and a destination picker — select or paste the destination address.

Fill in the amount and optional memo, then click **Mint tokens**.

![Mint Tokens modal with amount and memo filled in](/images/tokens/mint-modal-filled.png)

Confirm the on-chain submission in the confirmation prompt.

![Mint tokens confirmation dialog — click Mint now to submit the transaction on-chain](/images/tokens/mint-confirm.png)

Once confirmed, the mint appears in the Transactions table with a `confirmed` status and a "Mint transaction finalized." toast appears.

![Operations tab showing confirmed mint entry and Mint transaction finalized toast](/images/tokens/mint-confirmed.png)

</Tab>
<Tab value="API">

```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_abc123/mint \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: mint-001" \
  -d '{
    "signingCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_abc123",
    "mint": {
      "destination": "7xKXz...9fGh",
      "amount": "1000",
      "memo": "Initial distribution"
    }
  }'
```

```typescript title="mint-tokens.ts"
const res = await fetch(
  "https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_abc123/mint",
  {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: "Bearer sf_...",
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Idempotency-Key": "mint-001",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      signingCustodyWalletId: "cwlt_abc123",
      mint: {
        destination: "7xKXz...9fGh",
        amount: "1000",
        memo: "Initial distribution",
      },
    }),
  }
);
```

Control priority with `options.priorityFee`: `"none"`, `"low"`, `"medium"`, `"high"`, or a micro-lamport value.

</Tab>
</Tabs>
</StepPanel>

</Step>

<Step number={3} title="Burn tokens">

Reduce supply by burning from an account your wallet controls. Use force-burn to burn from any holder account without their signature.

<StepPanel>
<Tabs items={["UI", "API"]} groupId="how-it-works">
<Tab value="UI">

Click **Burn**. A modal shows the signer and a source field — select the wallet holding the tokens you want to remove.

![Burn Tokens modal with empty source field](/images/tokens/burn-modal-empty.png)

Select the source wallet from the dropdown.

![Burn Tokens modal with source wallet dropdown open](/images/tokens/burn-modal-source.png)

Fill in the amount and optional memo, then click **Burn tokens**.

![Burn Tokens modal filled with source, amount, and memo](/images/tokens/burn-modal-filled.png)

Confirm the on-chain submission in the confirmation prompt.

![Burn tokens confirmation dialog](/images/tokens/burn-confirm.png)

The "Burn transaction finalized." toast appears and the burn shows as confirmed in the Transactions table.

![Operations tab showing confirmed burn transaction and finalized toast](/images/tokens/burn-confirmed.png)

For **Force burn** (requires `tokens:admin`), use the Compliance tab instead of the Operations tab — force-burn lets admins remove tokens from any holder account without their signature.

</Tab>
<Tab value="API">

**Burn from a controlled account:**

```typescript title="burn-tokens.ts"
await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_abc123/burn", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: "Bearer sf_...",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Idempotency-Key": "burn-001",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    signingCustodyWalletId: "cwlt_abc123",
    burn: { source: "3xYZa...2aBc", amount: "250", memo: "Redemption" },
  }),
});
```

**Force-burn from any holder** (requires `tokens:admin`):

```typescript title="force-burn-tokens.ts"
await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_abc123/force-burn", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: "Bearer sf_...",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Idempotency-Key": "force-burn-001",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    signingCustodyWalletId: "cwlt_abc123",
    forceBurn: { source: "3xYZa...2aBc", amount: "250", memo: "Compliance action" },
  }),
});
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>
</StepPanel>

</Step>

<Step number={4} title="Refresh supply">

After minting or burning, refresh the cached supply total.

<StepPanel>
<Tabs items={["UI", "API"]} groupId="how-it-works">
<Tab value="UI">

The dashboard refreshes supply automatically after a confirmed operation. The Transactions table shows all completed operations — deploy, mint, and burn — each with a `confirmed` status.

![Operations tab showing confirmed burn, mint, and deploy transactions](/images/tokens/operations-history.png)

Reload the token detail page if the displayed supply value appears stale.

</Tab>
<Tab value="API">

```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_abc123/supply/refresh \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..."
```

Safe to include in automated post-mint workflows.

</Tab>
</Tabs>
</StepPanel>

</Step>

</HowItWorks>
